# Results — Study 894 (Trend Overlay on 60/40)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The rule under test: lay a
200-day trend filter over the balanced book — hold the 60% SPY leg when SPY is above its
200-day MA (else cash/BIL), hold the 40% IEF leg when IEF is above its own 200-day MA
(else cash) — and ask whether it **cuts drawdown while keeping most of the return**,
graded excess-of-cash vs excess-of-cash against the static 60/40. Offline & deterministic
once cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number. As-of
**2026-06-30** (the last complete calendar month; the partial current month is dropped).
Fingerprint `0dd2af7e1636` (SPY/IEF/AGG/BIL Close).*

Sample as-of 2026-06-30; Fingerprint `0dd2af7e1636`.

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily total-return Close (`auto_adjust=True`), **SPY / IEF / AGG / BIL**, 2007-05-30 → 2026-06-30, **4,802** aligned rows |
| Book | static **60% SPY / 40% IEF**, rebalanced to weight (the balanced-book benchmark); AGG is fetched as a bond-proxy robustness alternative to IEF |
| Cash leg | **BIL** (1-3m T-bills, total return) — both arms are measured **excess of BIL**, so the race strips out the level of short rates |
| Signal | each leg's close vs its **200-day simple moving average**, known at the close of `t−1` (one `shift`), acted on at `t`; the leg sits in **BIL** when below its MA. The 200-day MA warm-up is dropped so both arms race on an identical 4,602-day window |
| Costs | one-way switching cost × NAV fraction that flips per rebalance (**3 bps** headline; a 0/1/3/5 bps grid). Plus an optional short-term-gains **tax drag** on the gains realised each time a leg is forced to cash — a friction a buy-and-hold 60/40 never pays |
| Statistics | excess-vs-excess Sharpe race; Newey-West (HAC, 10-lag) *t* on the daily return difference; a **paired block-bootstrap** CI for the Sharpe advantage; a two-era cut; a calendar table; a 12-seed synthetic positive control |

**Short history — named on the Signal axis.** The cash leg **BIL launched 2007-05-25**, so
the balanced book here spans only ~2007-2026 (~19 years, one deep bear each in equities
[2008] and bonds [2022]). A single-crash sample gives a trend rule its best possible look;
the era cut below is the honest guard.

## The headline — trend-overlaid 60/40 vs static 60/40 (excess of BIL, n = 4,602 days)

| quantity | overlay (gross) | static 60/40 | difference |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| **excess Sharpe** | **0.823** | 0.689 | **+0.134** |
| max drawdown | **−12.5%** | −30.8% | **+18.3 pp shallower** |
| annualised vol | 6.9% | 11.4% | −4.5 pp |
| CAGR | 6.94% | 8.87% | **−1.93 pp/yr** |
| mean return diff | — | — | **−0.87 bps/day** (NW *t* = **−1.18**) |

The overlay does exactly what a trend filter is *supposed* to do: it **roughly halves the
drawdown and the volatility** (−12.5% vs −30.8%; 6.9% vs 11.4%). The excess Sharpe is
nominally higher (0.82 vs 0.69). But it buys that calm by **giving up ~1.9 pp/yr of
return** — the daily return difference is *negative* and statistically insignificant
(−0.87 bps/day, NW *t* = −1.18). This is the classic overlay trade-off: less risk, less
return; a higher Sharpe that rests entirely on the vol cut, not on out-earning the book.

## Is the Sharpe advantage real? Paired block-bootstrap (gross)

| quantity | value |
|---|--:|
| Sharpe advantage (overlay − static) | **+0.134** |
| 95% CI (paired circular block bootstrap) | **[−0.242, +0.517]** |
| P(advantage > 0) | **0.744** |
| return-difference mean (95% CI) | −0.87 bps/day ([−2.23, +0.59]) |

The Sharpe advantage's confidence interval **straddles zero** (the overlay out-Sharpes the
static book in only ~74% of resamples), and the return-difference CI contains zero too. So
the risk-adjusted *outperformance* is **not statistically distinguishable from zero** — the
drawdown/vol reduction is real, but "a higher Sharpe" is not a robust claim on this tape.

## Robustness — two eras (split 2017-01-01), gross

| era | Sharpe advantage | DD cut | overlay Sharpe / static |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 2007-2016 (n=2,217) | **+0.204** | +21.3 pp | 0.87 / 0.66 |
| 2017-2026 (n=2,385) | **+0.071** | +8.5 pp | 0.79 / 0.72 |

The advantage is **front-loaded**: most of it comes from ducking the 2008 crash. Post-2017
the Sharpe advantage fades to +0.07 and the drawdown cut shrinks from 21 pp to 8 pp. The
drawdown benefit is positive in *both* eras (the one durable, mechanical fact); the Sharpe
edge is not — it decays as the sample leaves 2008 behind.

## Calendar years — where the edge lives (net of 3 bps switching)

| year | overlay | static 60/40 | difference |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| **2008** | **+2.1%** | −13.2% | **+15.2 pp** |
| 2018 | +1.5% | −2.0% | +3.5 pp |
| **2022** | **−8.5%** | −16.4% | **+7.9 pp** |

The two years the overlay earns its keep are the two big balanced-book drawdowns (2008
equities, 2022 the bond-and-stock double-down). In every calm year it lags by the drag of
sitting in cash on false signals. It is a **tail-insurance overlay**, not a return engine.

## The timer — Sharpe advantage & DD cut across a cost grid (net, no tax)

| one-way cost | Sharpe advantage | DD cut | CAGR (overlay / static) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 bps | +0.134 | +18.3 pp | 6.94% / 8.87% |
| 1 bp | +0.124 | +18.1 pp | 6.87% / 8.87% |
| **3 bps** | **+0.104** | +17.8 pp | 6.72% / 8.87% |
| 5 bps | +0.084 | +17.5 pp | 6.57% / 8.87% |

Switching costs are **minor** — a 200-day rule flips a handful of times a decade, so even
5 bps one-way only shaves the Sharpe advantage from 0.13 to 0.08. **Tax is the killer:**

| friction | Sharpe advantage | DD cut | CAGR (overlay) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 3 bps switching only | +0.104 | +17.8 pp | 6.72% |
| 3 bps + 15% ST tax | −0.090 | +14.5 pp | 5.12% |
| **3 bps + 25% ST tax** | **−0.285** | +11.2 pp | 4.12% |

Because every forced move to cash **realises** a short-term gain that a buy-and-hold 60/40
defers, a taxable investor at a 25% short-term rate sees the (already-thin) Sharpe edge go
**negative** — the drawdown protection survives, but the risk-adjusted edge does not.

## Synthetic positive control — the machinery is unbiased

Deterministic seeded three-asset world; the equity leg has deep, persistent bear regimes
(`edge=1`) the 200-day filter can duck, or none at all (`edge=0`, the null). No network.

| world | Sharpe advantage | DD cut |
|---|--:|--:|
| planted (`edge=1`), 12 seeds | mean **+0.31**, positive in **11/12** | +40.9 pp |
| null (`edge=0`), 12 seeds | mean **+0.04** (no bear to duck) | — |

When deep bears exist the overlay recovers a genuine Sharpe pickup **and** a large drawdown
cut; on the null it does neither. *(A faithful-engine / power check only — never cited in
support of the real-tape stamp.)*

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The trend overlay delivers a **real, robust, mechanical drawdown and
  volatility reduction** (max DD −12.5% vs −30.8%, a ~18 pp cut; vol 6.9% vs 11.4%; the DD
  cut is positive in **both** eras). That much is genuine. But the headline claim — that it
  *cuts drawdown while keeping the return*, with a Sharpe **advantage** — does not clear a
  robust bar: the +0.13 Sharpe edge's bootstrap CI **straddles zero** ([−0.24, +0.52],
  P>0 = 0.74), the daily return difference is *negative* and insignificant (−0.87 bps/day,
  NW *t* = −1.18 — you give up ~1.9 pp/yr of CAGR), and the advantage is **front-loaded on
  2008** and fades to +0.07 post-2017. Real risk reduction, no robust risk-adjusted
  outperformance. *Short history (BIL from 2007) flatters a one-crash trend rule — named on
  the Signal axis.*
- **Tradability — FRAGILE.** As a **de-risking tool** the overlay is cheap and bankable:
  switching costs are trivial (5 bps one-way only trims the Sharpe advantage 0.13→0.08), so
  a tax-deferred account really does get a calmer ride net of costs. But there is **no
  robust net Sharpe outperformance** to bank: a modest **15% short-term tax already flips
  the Sharpe advantage negative** (−0.09), 25% takes it to −0.29, and the edge is era-decaying.
  Real-but-thin, tax-eaten, and reliant on the next big drawdown arriving — **Fragile**, not
  Investable (the drawdown protection survives costs, which is why it is not a Mirage).
